prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which have taken the precision of time measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement advance in the plainest sense: Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift, so many atoms can be interrogated at once with long coherence, and Ye's group turned this into fractional uncertainties and stabilities near 1e-18 with a fully understood systematics budget. That changes what can be measured, from tests of constants and relativity to relativistic geodesy and the redefinition of the second. All eight of us rank it in the top six, and independent groups (JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) reproduce and compare clocks at this level, so the result does not rest on a single laboratory. The credit is also unusually clean: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking it to the limit and into many-body regimes. I would keep the prize to this single achievement, because it is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize and needs no stretching of the citation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field is not yet finished. The SI second has not been redefined, and one can argue the committee should wait for that, or that optical clocks are an engineering refinement of atomic-clock ideas already recognised (Ramsey, Hall and Haensch, Wineland). Credit is also not perfectly confined to two people: Lemonde, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups (Wineland's NIST, PTB) contributed, and Ye's role partly rests on combs and ultrastable cavities that were built by others. There is a further sociological risk that precision metrology reads as less exciting than a new phase of matter or a new astronomical window.

responses.point: Pearce places IceCube and the high-energy astrophysical neutrino flux (B014) first, as an observational window built by instrument builders, and ranks the lattice clocks second.
responses.response: I agree with the criterion, since I value instruments that open a new way of observing nature, and the diffuse flux is well established. Where I differ is on attribution. IceCube is a very large collaboration with AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES precursors, and the neutrino sources are still only partly identified (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane). A pair of names for a detector this size involves more judgement than Katori and Ye, where concept and demonstration trace to two people. I would not oppose B014 later, but I think B015 is ready now and B014 gains by waiting for further source identifications.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators, the quantum spin Hall effect and the quantum anomalous Hall effect (B003) first, as a case where theory and experiment reinforced each other, with Kane, Molenkamp and Xue as laureates, and ranks lattice clocks fourth.
responses.response: The theory-experiment fit in B003 is real, and fifteen years of replication is persuasive even to a non-specialist. My reservation is the attribution you also note: Mele, Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang have strong claims, Zhang has died, and this candidate overlaps B018. If the committee cannot settle those cuts, the prize risks being contested from the day it is announced. The clock credit has no comparable ambiguity. I would also ask the condensed-matter members whether the 2016 topological-phase prize already covers a large part of the conceptual novelty. I am open to B003 as a second part if the names can be fixed, but a prize with only three persons leaves little room next to Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first together with me, stresses the precision-atomic-physics quality, the thorough understanding of systematic shifts and ripe timing, and ranks circuit QED fourth, partly because of the 2025 prize overlap.
responses.response: We agree on B015, but I should not let agreement from two atomic physicists pass for consensus. A fair test is whether non-AMO members find the case convincing, and Mehlig ranks it only sixth and cites overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes. On circuit QED I share your concern about the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits. I would add that the 2025 prize was about the quantum behaviour of a circuit, whereas circuit QED is about coupling and readout, so it is not a duplicate, but the committee will still be asked about it.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems (B005) first for being exact, universal and rigorously provable, and ranks the lattice clocks sixth, noting the closeness to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I take the point about universal statements, and fluctuation theorems are tested experimentally. Still, B005 has no other first-place support and the credit is the most contested on the list: you yourself note that Gallavotti, Cohen, Kurchan, Lebowitz-Spohn and Hatano-Sasa have competing claims, so a clean three-person split is not available. On the overlap, the lattice clock needs a distinct ingredient, the magic wavelength, which the comb and ion-clock prizes did not provide. Lattice clocks reach stability that neither trapped-ion nor earlier neutral-atom clocks matched, and that difference is measurable.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B039) first as the foundational architecture of superconducting processors, and places trapped-ion computation (B009) third and lattice clocks fifth.
responses.response: I accept that circuit QED is a clean new regime and that it is reproduced everywhere. My questions are the ones you raise yourself: Girvin and Huang are not credited, so the theory share is unresolved, and the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits is a near neighbour. I also rank B039 below B009 because ion experiments have the longer coherence times and the higher gate fidelities that I treat as the benchmark. A fair share of what makes circuit QED a platform is engineering development, including the transmon, which is not credited here.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second before recognising optical lattice clocks, or treat the physics as already established.

How much of Ye's contribution is distinct from the frequency-comb and ultrastable-cavity work already recognised in 2005, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto or ion-clock groups should be considered for the citation.
Whether the non-AMO members regard precision metrology as sufficiently discovery-like, given the low placement by Mehlig and Eriksson.
If B009 is chosen as an alternative, how to treat Wineland's 2012 prize and Monroe's experimental role when only Cirac, Zoller and Blatt are credited.
statement.conflict_note: A possible personal connection: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Jun Ye is a long-standing JILA colleague of that group and was trained in Hall's lab, so I have an indirect scientific link to the candidate's milieu, though no collaboration with Katori or Ye is evident from my profile. I also lead quantum sensing in the Chalmers-led WACQT, which overlaps institutionally with Johansson's home institution and with the superconducting-circuit platform of B039. The committee may wish to consider whether either point requires recusal; I do not think the first does, but I flag it.
